item.mechanism: Partial dislocation motion is hindered by friction caused by lattice parameter differences among constituent atoms, leading to hardening and reduced ductility compared to single-element nanowires.
item.supporting_observation: The motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to single element metallic nanowires like Ag where this friction is absent; not tested for non-cryogenic temperatures in this specific context of friction hindrance.
item.alternatives_considered: Nucleation and propagation of partial dislocations in single element metallic nanowires (e.g., Ag) which enable superplasticity without such friction.
quotes: In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility.

At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity.

item.mechanism: Superplasticity in Ag nanowires is driven by (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior enabled by partial dislocation nucleation and propagation.
item.supporting_observation: The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior.
item.scope_limits: At elevated temperatures (300 K and 1000 K), twin boundary propagation is retarded, and complete transformation is not possible, leading to failure by necking.
item.alternatives_considered: Deformation twinning and dislocation slip at higher temperatures which do not result in complete cross-section reorientation.
quotes: The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior.
At elevated temperatures, the propagation of twin boundaries is retarded due to thermal vibrations and complete transformation from (110) to (100) phase is not possible.

item.mechanism: Exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs in HEA nanowires result from synergistic interactions of deformation twinning, FCC-HCP phase transformation, and cross-section reorientation.
item.operating_conditions: Cryogenic temperatures (77 K) and high temperatures (up to 1000 K), tensile deformation
item.supporting_observation: Mechanical properties of HEA nanowires are better than Ag nanowires due to synergistic interactions of deformation twinning, FCC-HCP phase transformation, and the special reorientation of the cross-section.
item.scope_limits: The specific synergy varies with temperature; at 1000 K, phase transformation induced plasticity becomes more dominant than twinning.
item.alternatives_considered: Single mechanism dominance (e.g., only twinning in Ag at low temp) which yields different mechanical outcomes.
quotes: Mechanical properties of HEA nanowires are better than Ag nanowires due to synergistic interactions of deformation twinning, FCC-HCP phase transformation, and the special reorientation of the cross-section.
Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.

item.mechanism: Plasticity is achieved through the simultaneous activation of twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) at different stages and temperatures.
item.operating_conditions: Various temperatures (77 K, 300 K, 1000 K), tensile deformation
item.supporting_observation: Further examination reveals that simultaneous activation of twining induced plasticity and transformation induced plasticity are responsible for the plasticity at different stages and temperatures.
item.scope_limits: The dominance shifts with temperature; at 1000 K, TRIP is more dominant, while at 77 K, TWIP is dominant.
item.alternatives_considered: Isolated activation of either TWIP or TRIP without the synergistic effect.
quotes: Further examination reveals that simultaneous activation of twining induced plasticity and transformation induced plasticity are responsible for the plasticity at different stages and temperatures.
Simultaneous activation of twinning and martensitic transformation delays the onset of necking which results in a higher elongation to the fracture.

item.mechanism: Lomer Cottrell locks form via partial dislocation interactions, hindering dislocation motion and twin boundary propagation, thereby causing work hardening.
item.operating_conditions: Low temperatures (77 K, 300 K), tensile deformation
item.supporting_observation: The serration behavior is caused by the interaction of moving dislocations which further results in formation of Lomer Cottrell locks.
item.scope_limits: At high temperatures (1000 K), these locks can be unlocked by FCC-HCP transformation, changing their role from barriers to annihilation sites.
item.alternatives_considered: Simple dislocation glide without the formation of sessile locks.
quotes: The serration behavior is caused by the interaction of moving dislocations which further results in formation of Lomer Cottrell locks.
Lomer Cottrell locks enable a complex dislocation network and provide a strong resistance to the propagation of moving dislocations and are inherently responsible for the work hardening behavior.

item.mechanism: FCC-HCP martensitic transformation unlocks or annihilates Lomer Cottrell locks, allowing dislocations to move and providing secondary reinforcement via the HCP phase.
item.operating_conditions: High temperatures (1000 K) and later stages of deformation at 300 K, tensile deformation
item.supporting_observation: Due to the interaction of leading and trailing partial dislocations, Lomer Cottrell locks also form at 1000 K similar to the cases at low temperature. However, the Lomer Cottrell locks do not become impediments to the following dislocation motion but can be unlocked due to transformation into the HCP phase enabled by accumulation of stacking faults at the Lomer Cottrell locks.
item.scope_limits: At low temperatures (77 K), the transformation is limited and locks act primarily as barriers rather than being unlocked.
item.alternatives_considered: Permanent locking of dislocations leading to early failure without the TRIP effect.
quotes: However, the Lomer Cottrell locks do not become impediments to the following dislocation motion but can be unlocked due to transformation into the HCP phase enabled by accumulation of stacking faults at the Lomer Cottrell locks.
The transformed HCP phase results in the annihilation or unlocking of existing Lomer Cottrell junctions.

item.mechanism: Dislocation slip dominates over twinning at elevated temperatures due to increased intrinsic stacking fault energy and thermal activation.
item.system: Ag nanowires and CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires
item.operating_conditions: Elevated temperatures (300 K, 1000 K), tensile deformation
item.supporting_observation: Eventually, the deformation mechanism shifts from deformation twinning to dislocation slip at elevated temperatures.
item.scope_limits: This shift is temperature-dependent and does not occur at cryogenic temperatures where twinning is favored.
item.alternatives_considered: Twinning induced plasticity which is the dominant mechanism at low temperatures.
quotes: Eventually, the deformation mechanism shifts from deformation twinning to dislocation slip at elevated temperatures.
At 1000 K, owing to the thermal effect raising the nucleation frequency, the yielding occurs earlier with a value of only half of that at low temperature.
